analysis.one_liner: Bans lawsuits against gun makers and sellers for criminal misuse of their guns.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee at the end of the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred anyone — including cities and shooting victims — from suing lawful firearms manufacturers, dealers, or importers for harms caused when someone else misused a gun, and would have thrown out lawsuits already in court. It also would have banned any fee for a firearm background check and required federal authorities to immediately destroy records on gun buyers who pass a background check, with court remedies for violations. It was introduced by Senator Orrin Hatch with three Republican cosponsors in March 2000 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it stayed until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Firearms manufacturers, dealers, distributors, importers, and their trade associations, who would be shielded from civil liability — including suits then pending by cities seeking to recover gun-violence costs. Gun buyers would also save any background-check fee and gain a legal promise that records of passed checks are destroyed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade groups

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit any civil or equitable action in federal or state court against a lawful manufacturer or seller of a firearm, ammunition, or components for damages resulting from criminal or unlawful misuse by the buyer or a third party, with a carve-out only for sellers who knowingly sold a product they knew would be used to commit a crime [S2] [S3].
Any such lawsuit already pending on the date of enactment would have been dismissed immediately by the court where it was brought [S2] [S3].

The bill would ban charging or collecting any fee in connection with a firearm-transfer background check, retroactive to November 30, 1998, and would prohibit operating the instant background check system unless records on people who pass are destroyed immediately (except a unique identification number and its date), with civil remedies including punitive damages and attorney's fees for violations [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Shooting victims and their families, and cities that bore the costs of gun violence, would lose their main tool for holding the industry accountable in court — even in cases of negligent marketing or distribution, since the only exception is for sellers who knowingly supplied a gun for a crime. Governments would also give up any background-check fee revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shooting victims, their families, and cities

drawbacks.text: The bill would wipe out pending and future lawsuits against gun sellers not only for products that were defective, but also for claims based on how guns were marketed or distributed, since only sellers who knowingly supplied a product for a crime would remain subject to suit — leaving victims of negligent marketing or distribution with no remedy [S2] [S3].
Banning all background-check fees would remove funding that state agencies use to run checks, shifting those costs entirely to federal appropriations or leaving agencies short [S3].

Supporters argued the suits targeted lawful businesses for the crimes of others and threatened a constitutional right; the bill's findings state that industry-wide liability for third-party misuse is an abuse of the legal system and a burden on interstate commerce [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Gun buyers got real but modest promised benefits: no fees for background checks and destruction of records on passed checks. Against that, the bill's core effect was a sweeping shield for the gun industry: it would have ended the wave of municipal lawsuits over gun violence and blocked victims' suits even where a seller was negligent rather than knowingly criminal. On balance the bill primarily served the industry, and its death left existing lawsuits alive.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2000, and the committee never acted on it before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on March 22, 2000, joined by Senators Larry Craig and Bob Smith of New Hampshire [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, its only action beyond introduction [S5].
No committee markup, report, or floor vote ever occurred before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, cities and shooting victims kept the ability to sue gun makers and sellers, and the firearms industry did not get the immunity it sought; no one lost anything they already had.

for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Sens. Larry Craig and Bob Smith of New Hampshire

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only Republican sponsorship and no opposition actions; the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would reveal who supported or opposed it.

industries.note: The bill would have granted them near-total immunity from lawsuits over criminal misuse of their products, including suits then pending by cities, with an exception only for sellers who knowingly supplied a gun for a crime. Victims and cities would have been left with no way to recover for negligent marketing or distribution.
The bill explicitly extends the lawsuit ban to trade associations, protecting industry groups from being sued over industry practices.
Cities were bringing suits to recover the public costs of gun violence; the bill would have dismissed those cases and barred new ones, shifting those costs back onto taxpayers and victims.
The fee ban and record-destruction rules would save buyers small check fees and keep the government from retaining records on lawful purchases.
